title: Improving the prediction of bitumen’s density and thermal expansion by optimizing artificial neural networks with Optuna and TensorFlow☆
author: Assaf, Liu, et al.

steps.title: Assemble molecular models
steps.instruction: Create 197 bitumen‑based systems by selecting molecules from the Greenfield and Shisong libraries and packing each into a mixture of ~6000 atoms (≈80 molecules per sample). Match each system’s composition to experimental SARA fractions, elemental analysis, GPC profiles and FTIR spectra where available.

steps.title: Perform temperature sweep MD simulations
steps.instruction: For each assembled system run a virtual temperature sweep at nine discrete temperatures: –60, –20, 0, 25, 60, 120, 135, 160 and 200 °C. At each temperature execute four sequential phases: Heating → Equilibration → Extraction → Stability Assessment. Use the configuration at the end of the Extraction phase (a 5‑nanosecond NPT ensemble) as the data point for the dataset.

steps.title: Run LAMMPS simulations
steps.instruction: Conduct all MD simulations with LAMMPS using the Polymer Covalent Force Field (PCFF). Integrate atomic motion with the modified Nosé–Hoover thermostat via the fix npt command, applying a velocity‑drag factor of 1.0. Set temperature and pressure damping parameters to 500 timesteps, pressure to 101 325 Pa, and the integration timestep to 0.5 fs.

steps.title: Prepare LAMMPS input files
steps.instruction: Convert molecular structures to LAMMPS format: generate initial structures with SMI2PDB, convert to LAMMPS data files with PDB2DAT, and create the simulation scripts using Scymol.

steps.title: Execute simulations on DelftBlue
steps.instruction: Submit the LAMMPS jobs to the DelftBlue supercomputer using 16 Intel Xeon E5‑6248R cores with 1 GB memory per core. Expect ~3 h of compute time to add a new temperature point for an existing sample and ~24 h to generate a completely new sample across all nine temperatures.

steps.title: Construct final dataset
steps.instruction: Collect the 5‑ns NPT extraction configurations from all simulations, yielding 1773 distinct configurations (each chemically and/or conditionally unique) to be used for machine‑learning training.

steps.title: Define input features
steps.instruction: For each configuration build a 32‑element input vector: x₁‑x₃₀ are fractional atom‑type counts (ai/N, where N is total atoms), x₃₁ is the average molecular weight (range 200–1000 g mol⁻¹), and x₃₂ is temperature (range –60 °C to 200 °C).

steps.title: Split data into training and testing sets
steps.instruction: Create training‑testing splits using ratios from 70/30 to 90/10 in 5 % increments. Randomly assign samples according to the chosen ratio for each Optuna trial.

steps.title: Scale inputs and outputs
steps.instruction: For each trial randomly select a scaler for inputs and another for outputs from MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler, and MaxAbsScaler (categorical choice). Apply the selected scaler to the corresponding data.

steps.title: Configure Optuna hyperparameter search
steps.instruction: Run Optuna with 2048 trials per case study. Sample architecture (FCNN, WDNN, ResNet), sampler type (TPESampler, NSGAIISampler, GridSampler), loss function (Huber with δ 0.1–10, Log‑Cosh, MSE), learning‑rate, number of layers, neurons per layer, batch size, epochs, and any architecture‑specific parameters. Treat the loss function as a hyperparameter.

steps.title: Train ANN models
steps.instruction: For each trial train the selected ANN architecture on the training set using TensorFlow/Keras with the chosen loss function and optimizer. Record training loss and validation loss.

steps.title: Compute performance metrics
steps.instruction: After training evaluate the model on the testing set and calculate: Normalized MSE, Normalized MAE, R², Normalized MaxAE, and ΔR² (|R²_train – R²_test|).

steps.title: Filter models – Pareto front
steps.instruction: Identify Pareto‑optimal models where no other model simultaneously improves all five metrics. Discard all non‑Pareto models.

steps.title: Apply static threshold filters
steps.instruction: From the Pareto set retain only models meeting all thresholds: MSE ≤ 0.05, MAE ≤ 0.05, R² ≥ 0.99, MaxAE ≤ 0.05, ΔR² ≤ 0.01 (Δy = max(y) – min(y) for normalization).

steps.title: Perform physical consistency checks
steps.instruction: For each remaining model conduct three checks on the testing points:

substeps.instruction: Compute Wavelet High‑Frequency Energy Ew; accept if 0.005 ≤ Ew ≤ 0.03.
Compute Total Variation Norm TV; accept if 0.15 < TV < 15.
Count Monotonicity Flips M; accept only if M = 0.

steps.title: Interpolate between test points
steps.instruction: For every adjacent pair of test points generate 20 evenly spaced synthetic points using xi,j = xi + j·(xi+1 – xi)/20 (j = 1…20). Evaluate the three physical checks (Wavelet Energy, TV, Monotonicity Flips) on the predictions at these interpolated points. Retain models passing all checks.

steps.title: Assess extrapolation performance – input extension
steps.instruction: Extend each input variable by ±10 % beyond its original limits, generate 100 equally spaced points, and repeat the three physical checks. Omit any test that would produce impossible atom‑type fractions (e.g., negative values). Keep models that remain within the acceptable ranges.

steps.title: Assess extrapolation performance – unseen compounds
steps.instruction: Select 14 external molecules from PubChem with Takimoto similarity to the training set. Build MD models for each using the same Data Collection workflow, run LAMMPS simulations, and obtain reference densities and β values. Predict these properties with each candidate model and verify that all previous metric thresholds and physical checks are satisfied.

steps.title: Select final model based on inference speed
steps.instruction: Among models that passed all previous steps choose the one with the lowest inference time (measured per compound). Record that all architectures achieve ~100 ms inference; the WDNN architecture is fastest at 33.4 ms and is therefore selected.

steps.title: Predict target properties
steps.instruction: Using the selected WDNN model predict density (ρ) and thermal expansion coefficient (β) for any new bitumen composition and temperature within the defined ranges. For β you may either use the direct model output or compute β = –(1/ρ)·(∂ρ/∂T) from the predicted ρ(T) if desired.
